newsitem.title: UK: British minister makes pledge to Gulf War veterans.
newsitem.headline: British minister makes pledge to Gulf War veterans.

text.p: Britain's Armed Forces Minister Nicholas Soames pledged on Sunday the government would pay compensation to sick Gulf War veterans if negligence was proved.
Last week, Soames announced a new research programme into illnesses suffered by British servicemen in the 1991 conflict.

The three-year study funded by the Defence Ministry followed a government admission that, contrary to what ministers had said in the past, so-called organophosphate pesticides had been more widely used in the Gulf than had been thought.
Soames, writing in the News of the World tabloid on Sunday, said: "We will do all in our power to find out the truth.
"And if we are liable through our own actions for negligently harming our men and women, then of course we must pay compensation. We will not hesitate to do so."
The government's admission it gave misleading information to parliament on the use of pesticides and its decision to go ahead with the new study amounted to a significant shift of position.
The government has insisted there is no single syndrome to explain the illnesses of the Gulf War veterans.
But lawyers for more than 1,000 British veterans who say they are suffering from Gulf War syndrome said last month they they would issue writs against the Defence Ministry in January.

The veterans say evidence collected in the United States supports their argument that there is a syndrome caused by a "cocktail" of immunisations they were given to protect them against chemical and biological warfare and by the pesticides.
About 51,000 Britons were involved in the war against Iraq following President Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait.
Around 750 veterans have complained of chronic fatigue, asthma, depression and skin complaints. Some are now confined to wheelchairs and say their children have suffered birth defects.
